tasks.title: Sec A · 第 1 组
tasks.context: Questions 1 to 4 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

questions.stem: What do we learn about the man from the conversation?

options.A: He has distinguished himself in foreign service.
options.B: He is his country’s ambassador to Winopia.
options.C: He is currently an electrical engineer.
options.D: He craves attention from the media.

questions.stem: What does the man say the government of Winopia is probably undergoing?

options.B: A fundamental reform.
options.C: Some sort of political reorientation.
options.D: Some sort of crisis of legitimacy.

questions.stem: According to the man, how does one get a career in foreign relations?

options.A: All diplomats have more or less similar stories to tell.
options.B: It is a prerequisite to get some practice in diplomacy.
options.C: Different people can take different paths.
options.D: It is a must to first obtain a law degree.

questions.stem: What do the speakers mainly discuss by the end of the conversation?

options.A: Key skills required of a diplomat.
options.B: The making of an expert diplomat.
options.C: Diplomatic discourse and rhetoric.
options.D: Contributions by diplomatic envoys.

lines.t: Today’s special guest is Lord Blackwell, one of our country’s most experienced and distinguished career diplomats.
It’s my pleasure.
Our audience will be most interested in learning about a career in the foreign service.
However, before we talk about that, I’d like to ask you about the current developments hitting the news today regarding the Republic of Winopia.
What can you tell us?
I’m afraid I don’t know much beyond what we’ve all seen on the news.
It looks like the government of Winopia seems to be undergoing some sort of crisis of legitimacy and an interim administration has been transitionally established until a head of state is agreed on.
But my career work has mostly focused around the Continental spheres of Europe and the Americas, and thus I’ve never been involved with Winopian relations.
It’s for this reason that I don’t know anything on this matter beyond what we can all read in the newspapers.
Oh, I see.
Nevertheless, be rest assured that our export envoys at our consulate there will be closely monitoring the situation and I expect our bilateral relations with that country will not be affected.
So how does one get a career in foreign relations?
There are many different paths one can take.
All diplomats have their own story.
But in my case, I got a degree in electrical engineering followed by six years’ service in the Air Force.
Then I went to a law school and upon obtaining a degree in international law, I joined the diplomatic core where I’ve been for 22 years.
What would you say are the key skills one needs for the job?
There are so many.
Being a hard worker and good student is important--you never stop learning.
In addition, a diplomat needs to be very articulate in their discourse and rhetoric.
Whether it is diffusing tension or enacting policy, people and communication skills are vital.

tasks.title: Sec A · 第 2 组
tasks.context: Questions 5 to 8 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

questions.stem: Why does the man suggest they call it a day?

options.A: They have got their work done.
options.B: They both look tired.
options.C: They can meet again tomorrow anyway.
options.D: They are both anxious to go home.

questions.stem: What does the woman say is a little tough?

options.B: Two months devoted to the same contract.
options.C: Working two months without any progress.
options.D: The man’s long concentration on the project.

questions.stem: What does the man say the woman must be in thinking they’ll finish by next week?

options.B: Inspirational.
options.C: Exceptional.
options.D: Delusional.

questions.stem: What does the entire managerial hierarchy want to see according to the woman?

options.B: More support from the board members.
options.C: The early implementation of the project.
options.D: The alignment of all sections of the contract.

lines.t: It’s getting late and we’re both displaying signs of weariness.
I think we should call it a day and meet again tomorrow morning.
Oh, come on Jeff.
We are so close.
Don’t you think we’re almost done?
Let’s do two more hours, please.
One hour, then I’m going home.
OK, fine.
I think we are making good progress and that with a few more amendments we will be all done.
I’m sure looking forward to it.
I’m so tired of this project.
Don’t get me wrong--it’s a great professional opportunity for me and a milestone for the company, but it’s just been so long.
Yeah, two months working on nothing but the same contract is a little tough.
Nevertheless, I think that with a bit of luck we’ll be done by next week.
Ha!
You must be delusional.
You don’t think so?
No chance.
Sections four, five, eight and nine still have to be aligned in the new framework.
Then we need to proofread the whole thing and make sure all selling points are watertight.
But that will all take no more than a couple of days.
I wasn’t finished.
When we are done with it and send it upstairs, what do you think will happen?
What?
They’ll argue about it for like a month.
There’s always going to be the odd board member who intervenes and demands rectifications be made.
They might think they’re being helpful but in reality they’re being obstructive and hampering progress.
Oh Jeff, you’re too preoccupied and cynical.
It won’t be anywhere as bad as that.
You’ll see.
The entire managerial hierarchy wants to see this project implemented as soon as possible and the board too is virtually unanimous in its support.
Go on then, let’s stop there and meet up again, same time tomorrow.

tasks.title: Sec B · 第 3 组
tasks.context: Questions 9 to 11 are based on the passage you have just heard.

questions.stem: When can it be hard to know whom to believe?

options.A: When two employees propose contrary solutions to their dispute.
options.B: When two employees are directed by their respective manager.
options.C: When two people behave in an apparently clashing manner.
options.D: When two people tell different stories of the same event.

questions.stem: What does the speaker definitely recall about the dispute mentioned as an example?

options.B: How it happened.
options.C: What it was about.
options.D: When it was settled.

questions.stem: What did the speaker and his counterpart do when the two employees gave different accounts of the same event?

options.A: They intervened promptly lest their dispute escalate.
options.B: They tried to ascertain the actual facts of the matter.
options.C: They assumed the best about them and moved on.
options.D: They persuaded them to put their conflict aside.

lines.t: One thing I’ve learned in a quarter century of management is that there are ample gray areas in human behavior and that there may not always be clear right-or-wrong solutions to employee disputes.
When two people have different versions of the same event, it can be hard to know whom to believe.
One such circumstance always comes back to me.
It happened years ago and it’s a measure of the forgettable nature of the conflict that I no longer even recall what the dispute was about, but I definitely recall the resolution.
Two talented young executives, one of whom I was managing, had vastly different accounts of the same event and it seemed likely we’d never get to the truth.
We reached the deadlock.
And the manager of the other individual said, “Here’s something I learned from an excellent manager I once worked for.”
He used to say, “when in doubt, assume positive intent.”
And just like that, we had a path forward.
My counterpart and I agreed we might never ascertain the actual facts of the matter.
Quite likely there were elements of truth in both employees’ stories.
We agreed to monitor their actions and relationship going forward, but to intervene no further.
We assumed the best about both of them and moved on.
The result was that we were able to put the conflict behind us.
In fact, their problems didn’t recur.
Over the years this general approach has proved useful.
Whenever the truth is obscure, assuming positive intent and agreeing to move on can be a constructive decision.

tasks.title: Sec B · 第 4 组
tasks.context: Questions 12 to 15 are based on the passage you have just heard.

questions.stem: What do an increasing number of Americans do according to the passage?

options.B: Budget sensibly.
options.C: Enjoy cooking.
options.D: Shop at groceries.

questions.stem: What does Eddie Yoon think cooking is akin to?

options.B: Sewing.
options.C: Entertaining oneself.
options.D: Fashion designing.

questions.stem: What will Americans be able to do by making their own lunch?

options.B: Cut down expenses.
options.C: Eat more healthily.
options.D: Cultivate new hobbies.

questions.stem: What does the passage say signifies a host of challenges for America’s grocery industry?

options.B: People’s deteriorating family finances.
options.C: People’s strong aversion to junk foods.
options.D: People’s increasing dislike of cooking.

lines.t: For some Americans, going out to dinner is a treat, planned and budgeted for.
For others, it’s just a daily occurrence.
And that second group of people is becoming the majority, as the number of Americans who enjoy cooking is declining.
In the early 2000s, researcher Eddie Yoon conducted a survey to ascertain Americans’ attitudes to cooking.
The survey found that 15% of Americans loved to cook, 50% said they hated to cook and 35% reported mixed feelings.
When Yoon conducted the same survey 15 years later, only 10% of respondents reported a love of cooking, 45% said they hated it, and 45% had mixed feelings.
Yoon asserts cooking is akin to sewing.
As recently as the early 20th century, many Americans sewed their own clothing.
Today, the vast majority of Americans buy clothing; only a tiny minority still sew and they do it mainly as a hobby.
Yoon believes the number of home cooks will diminish in a similar fashion.
Currently, the average American household spends over $3,000 per year on dining out.
However, what people save in convenience, they lose in cash.
Take buying lunch on work days, for example.
People spend on average $10 per meal when they buy lunch.
Making your own lunch, meanwhile, will cost less.
One survey found people only spend on average $6.30 when they bring lunch prepared at home.
Americans’ growing aversion to spending time in the kitchen signifies a host of challenges for the grocery industry.
It’s likely to detrimentally impact family finances as well.

tasks.title: Sec C · 第 5 组
tasks.context: Questions 16 to 18 are based on the recording you have just heard.

questions.stem: What is the number one reason a bag ends up lost according to this talk?

options.A: Its owner’s flight is delayed because of bad weather.
options.B: Airlines cannot find its owner without an ID tag on it.
options.C: Airline staff have not correctly coded its destination tag.
options.D: Its owner has forgot to pick it up from the baggage claim.

questions.stem: What may happen to your baggage even when there are sophisticated automated systems?

options.A: Its tag may get torn off on the conveyor belt.
options.B: Its tag may get stuck in the sorting machine.
options.C: It may be sent to a wrong destination.
options.D: It may be picked up by someone else.

questions.stem: What does the speaker advise us to do at the end of the talk?

options.A: Purchase irretrievably lost things at auction.
options.B: Contact the airport staff to find our missing bag.
options.C: Get the airline agent’s phone number before boarding.
options.D: Avoid packing valuable items in our checked baggage.

lines.t: Every year, of the more than 2.5 billion bags checked onto flights worldwide, 26 million go missing.
And of that 26 million, 1 million never make it back to their original owner.
Bad weather and flight delays, miscoded destination tags, and some people simply forgetting to pick up one of their bags are a few of the reasons.
But the number one reason a bag ends up lost is that it has no ID tag and airlines don’t know to whom it belongs.
Transferring baggage from check-in to departure gates to arrival gates to baggage claim is a delicate piece of timing.
If the system moves too slowly, the bags won’t make connecting flights.
If it’s too fast, the bags may make the connection, but the passengers might miss the flight.
Each airport has its own way of allotting how much time a bag needs to move in transit.

Some airports have sophisticated automated systems, including scanners that read baggage labels, destination coded vehicles that load and unload the bags without stopping, and sorting machines that route baggage to the appropriate gate.
Even so, all that technology may not save your baggage tag from being torn off on the conveyor belt, making you the owner of a bag with no name.
Once a bag goes missing and the passenger files a claim, the bag is declared mishandled by the carrier.
Mishandled refers to bags that have been delayed, lost, stolen or damaged.
Most delayed bags are only one flight behind their owners and can be delivered within 24 hours.
The other bags are examined by airline employees for clues to their ownership and destination.
If the mystery is solved, those bags are returned to their owners within four or five days.
Bags with no destination code or identification tag are shipped to a central warehouse and undergo a comprehensive baggage tracing process over the next 90 days.
Airlines inventory their mishandled baggage, and many use a database to match the contents with owners’ descriptions.
It takes about three months to go from missing in action to irretrievably lost.
Once that happens, the bags are donated to charity, sold at auction, or purchased by a company which sells them to the public.
So never pack anything of real value in your checked baggage and make sure your name is on the bag along with your phone number so an agent can contact you.

tasks.title: Sec C · 第 6 组
tasks.context: Questions 19 to 21 are based on the recording you have just heard.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say about using one smartphone during a face-to-face conversation?

options.B: It can be especially disappointing.
options.C: It can be socially harmful.
options.D: It can be really embarrassing.

questions.stem: How did the participants in the new study respond regarding phone use during social interactions?

options.B: They held a negative view towards it.
options.C: They were concerned with its effects.
options.D: They saw it as a sign of social evolution.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say can result from the common behavior of using phones during face-to-face conversations?

options.B: Ill effects on one’s sense of pride.
options.C: Poor relationships with others.
options.D: Vicious cycles of detachment.

lines.t: You’ve probably been with someone who ignored you while interacting with his or her smartphone, and you’ve probably engaged in this behavior yourself.
In a recent survey, nine out of ten respondents said they’d used their smartphone during their most recent social activity.
There’s also evidence that this behavior is socially harmful.
It can leave people less satisfied with their face-to-face interactions, and it can generate feelings of resentment and jealousy.
Now, the Journal of Applied Social Psychology has published a new study exploring the reasons for these effects.
The study included 128 mostly female student participants.
The participants watched a three-minute animation in which two cartoon figures interacted and engaged in a conversation.
The conversation couldn’t be heard, but could be detected through mouth movements.
Participants had to imagine themselves as the closest figure in the video, and then make judgments about the conversations and how they felt about their conversation partners.
In one version of the experiment, the phone of the participant’s conversation partner remained unused on the table throughout the conversation.
In another version, their partner’s attention was quickly drawn to something on their phone, and they spent the rest of the time interacting with their phone.
A third version involved the participant’s partner alternating between periods of interaction with their phone and periods where they ignored their phone.
If you’ve experienced the similar situation, you probably won’t be surprised by the results of the experiments.
The participants had a negative view of phone use during social interactions.
The more it was present, the worse they considered both the quality of the interaction and the quality of the relationship.
The researchers believed that focusing on one’s phone instead of the person one is with has this effect because it’s seen as a form of social exclusion.
They assert that the behavior is analogous to when people have no choice but to eat alone in the school cafeteria.
The twist is that this exclusion occurs while sharing a physical encounter and having a conversation.
Researchers found that the behavior had adverse effects on participants’ sense of belonging, need for meaning and self-esteem.
These negative effects are similar to those caused by traditional forms of social exclusion.
The new findings are important because they elaborate our understanding of a subtle but common aspect of our daily experience.
This common behavior can create vicious cycles of detachment even as we try to connect with others.

tasks.title: Sec C · 第 7 组
tasks.context: Questions 22 to 25 are based on the recording you have just heard.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say travelers commonly complain about?

options.A: The ill treatment they get as tourists.
options.B: The nonprofessional business they see.
options.C: The impersonal accommodations.
options.D: The many adventures on their way.

questions.stem: What is said about bed-and-breakfast arrangements?

options.A: They have been the classic way to visit Europe.
options.B: They attract tourists with location and decoration.
options.C: They have long been competing with chain hotels.
options.D: They are in fact a completely new idea in America.

questions.stem: What is the first thing you have to consider if you want to start a B&B business?

options.B: Your family’s consent.
options.C: Your property.
options.D: Your personality.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say potential B&B hosts must be realistic about?

options.B: The number of guests to receive.
options.C: The facilities to provide.
options.D: Opportunities for income.

lines.t: More and more people travel for a variety of reasons.
Many are tourists, but many venture for some personal or professional business.
Whatever the reason for traveling, a common complaint of travelers is the impersonal accommodations they find.
After spending five consecutive nights in five similar hotels, the business traveler may find it difficult to remember what happened from day to day or even what towns were visited.
And the tourists may get the mistaken impression that all cities are pretty much the same, at least as far as decoration, food and service are concerned.
To combat this sense of impersonal sameness, travelers are taking advantage of in-home hospitality or bed-and-breakfast arrangements.
B&Bs, I mean, bed-and-breakfast arrangements, are private homes which offer lodging and breakfast in a very personalized friendly setting.
For decades, B&Bs have been the classic way to visit Europe, especially the British Isles.
And in fact, they are not really a new idea in America.
The tradition dates back to colonial times when inns were few and far between, and the weary traveler had to depend on the kindness of strangers for a meal and a bed.
But the revival of B&Bs as desirable accommodations is a fairly recent phenomenon.
If the idea of operating a B&B arouses your interest, there are several factors to consider before plunging into this business.
The first consideration is your property, not only the building itself, but the location.
If you live near a famous historical site or in a popular destination such as New York City or Washington D.C., your home can be fairly simple yet still do well as a B&B.

On the other hand, if your home is architecturally unique or has facilities for the traveler such as a private entrance, private bath or swimming pool, people may be willing to go some distance to reach you.
Another important factor is the lifestyle of you and your family.

You must take into account whether all members of the family truly enjoy visitors, want to repeatedly discuss local sites and activities, and have the time and energy to handle the additional cooking, cleaning, laundry and the book keeping involved.
The final consideration is a financial one.
Potential B&B hosts must be realistic about opportunities for income.
While B&Bs usually have low initial costs, experts estimate it would take at least five rooms rented regularly for the host to earn a living from B&B.
